fields.Front: You are standing up an insurance claims-processing pipeline on Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1. Two failures appear on the first day of testing and recur on every attempt: each converse call that names its Claude model by the base model ID is rejected with an HTTP 400 error saying that invoking that model ID with on-demand throughput isn't supported, and each call to the Titan Text Embeddings model is rejected with an error that your account does not have access to that model. A teammate's pipeline in a different AWS account calls the same embeddings model without errors. Which TWO changes resolve these failures? (Select TWO.) A. Wrap both calls in a retry with exponential backoff, since the errors indicate transient capacity problems in the region. B. Switch from converse to invoke_model, which accepts base model IDs and models that are not yet enabled for the account. C. Replace the base model ID with the model's cross-region inference profile ID so Bedrock can route the request to a region that serves the model. D. Enable access to the Titan embeddings model for your own AWS account, because Bedrock determines model access separately for each account.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C and D. Option C addresses the first failure: Bedrock offers newer Claude models through cross-region inference rather than on-demand throughput, so a request that passes the base model ID is rejected; an inference profile ID (the base model ID with a prefix such as us.) names a profile that defines the model and the Regions Bedrock can route the request to. Option D addresses the second failure: access to a foundation model is determined separately for each AWS account, which is why the same embeddings model works from a teammate's account but not from yours. Option A treats deterministic configuration errors as transient and would retry forever. Option B changes the invocation API, but model IDs and account access are enforced the same way for invoke_model. Currency note (Oct 2026): AWS docs now say access to many Bedrock models is enabled by default and point to the caller's IAM permissions for an access-denied error; the console's Model access page is now described only for AWS GovCloud (US). Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) References: • Claude on Amazon Bedrock (Opus 4.6 and earlier) — API model IDs • Cross-region inference (AWS docs) • Request access to models (AWS docs)

fields.Front: A developer on your financial-services document intake team ports a helper from a prior project that used the Anthropic Python SDK. On Bedrock the helper's client.converse(...) call succeeds, but reading the generated text with response["content"][0]["text"] raises a KeyError on every request. What is the correct way to read the generated text from the Converse response? A. json.loads(response["body"].read())["content"][0]["text"], since Bedrock returns a streaming body that must be decoded first. B. response["completion"], which Converse populates with the concatenated text of all parts. C. response["content"][0]["text"] after adding anthropic_version to the request, which switches Converse to the Anthropic response format. D. response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"], because Converse wraps the assistant message in an output envelope.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: the Converse API returns an envelope in which the assistant message lives under output and then message, and the message's content is a list of parts, so the first text part is at response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]. The Bedrock API and the Anthropic API are different services with different SDKs and response shapes, which is why the ported path fails. Option A describes reading an invoke_model response body, not a Converse response. Option B names a field Converse does not return. Option C mixes the two APIs; anthropic_version belongs in the native invoke_model request body and does not change Converse's envelope. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) References: • Converse API (AWS docs) — Converse response • Converse API reference (AWS docs) — Response Syntax • Claude on Amazon Bedrock (Opus 4.6 and earlier) — Making requests

fields.Front: Your team copies a request from the Anthropic Messages API documentation into a boto3 converse call for a healthcare intake assistant, passing system="You are an intake assistant..." as a plain string and temperature=0.2 as a top-level keyword argument. boto3 rejects the call with a parameter validation error before any request leaves the machine. The service's response handling is already written for the Converse API. What is the most direct fix? A. Move both values into additionalModelRequestFields and drop the top-level system and temperature arguments from the call. B. Switch the call to invoke_model and send both values in a JSON request body that carries an anthropic_version field. C. Pass the system prompt as system=[{"text": "..."}] and move the temperature into inferenceConfig={"temperature": 0.2}. D. Keep both arguments as written and set the client's region_name to a Region that hosts the model you are calling.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The Converse API defines its own request shape: the system prompt is a list of content parts ([{"text": ...}]), and sampling settings such as temperature and stop sequences live inside inferenceConfig. Requests written against the Anthropic API's shape fail boto3's client-side validation because the two services use different SDKs and parameter names. Option A moves standard Converse settings into additionalModelRequestFields, which exists for model-specific fields that Converse does not model natively, not for standard fields it already defines. Option B abandons the Converse API that the service's response handling is built on; Converse supports system prompts, and invoke_model would require rewriting the entire request body. Option D addresses a routing problem, but this error is raised locally before any request reaches a Region, so changing region_name cannot clear it. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) References: • Converse API reference (AWS docs) — Request Body • Converse API (AWS docs) — Request • Anthropic Claude Messages API request and response (AWS docs)

fields.Front: Your financial-services intake service calls Claude through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. It builds each request by appending a user message containing the full text of a 30-page filing and then appending a second user message containing the analyst's question. Every call fails with a validation error stating that the conversation must alternate between user and assistant roles. How should the request be restructured? A. Send the filing and the question as two text parts inside the content list of a single user message. B. Insert a placeholder assistant message such as Understood. between the two user messages so the roles alternate. C. Send the filing in one converse call, then send the question in a second call, relying on Bedrock to retain the first. D. Move the filing text into the system parameter as a string and keep the question as the only user message.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: a message's content is a list precisely so that one message can carry several parts (multiple text parts, or text alongside documents or images). Placing the filing and the question as two parts of one user message satisfies the alternation rule that Converse enforces while keeping both in the same turn. Option B would get past validation, but only by fabricating an assistant turn that Claude never produced, when a single message can already carry both parts. Option C fails because Bedrock is stateless and stores nothing between calls; the second request would contain no filing. Option D fails validation in a new way, because on Converse the system parameter is a list of content blocks rather than a string, and it moves per-request document content into a field meant for standing instructions. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) References: • Converse API (AWS docs) — messages • Message — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Using the Messages API — Multiple conversational turns

fields.Front: A new engineer on your claims pipeline creates the client with boto3.client("bedrock", region_name="us-west-2"). Calls that list the available foundation models work, but client.converse(...) raises AttributeError: 'Bedrock' object has no attribute 'converse'. What is the cause? A. The installed boto3 release predates the Converse API; upgrading boto3 would add a converse method to the bedrock client. B. Converse must first be enabled for each model in the Bedrock console, and only then does boto3 expose the method on the client. C. The us-west-2 Region does not offer the Converse API, so boto3 leaves the method off any client created for that Region. D. The converse operation belongs to the bedrock-runtime client, which invokes models; bedrock is the control-plane client.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Bedrock exposes two boto3 clients: bedrock is the control plane (listing models, managing access and jobs), while bedrock-runtime is the data plane that actually invokes models through converse, converse_stream, and invoke_model. Code that sends Converse requests connects to the Bedrock runtime for exactly this reason. Option A is wrong because the method never lives on the control-plane client regardless of version. Option B confuses model access enablement, which produces an access error at call time, with a missing SDK method. Option C is wrong because boto3 builds client methods from the service definition, not from regional support. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) References: • Converse API (AWS docs) • Bedrock API Reference — Welcome (AWS docs) • Claude on Amazon Bedrock (Opus 4.6 and earlier) — List available models

fields.Front: A healthcare intake assistant your team runs on Amazon Bedrock uses a shared chat() helper that always passes system=[{"text": system_prompt}] to converse. Callers that have no system prompt pass an empty string, and 100% of those calls fail with a validation error that the system prompt must contain at least one character. What is the most appropriate change to the helper? A. Default the system prompt to a single space so the parameter is never empty and validation always passes. B. Build the request parameters as a dictionary and add the system key only when a non-empty prompt is supplied. C. Move the callers' instructions into the first user message and remove the system parameter entirely. D. Wrap the call in a retry that strips the system parameter after the first validation failure.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Bedrock requires that a system prompt, if present, contain at least one character, so the clean design is a helper whose system prompt defaults to None and that includes the system key in the converse parameters only when a prompt is provided. Option A sends a meaningless one-character prompt on every call just to satisfy validation. Option C removes the system prompt for everyone, discarding the role-based control that callers who do supply a prompt rely on. Option D turns a known, deterministic validation rule into a failed request plus a retry on every call. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) References: • SystemContentBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Converse API (AWS docs) — system • Prompting best practices — Give Claude a role

fields.Front: Your claims-processing agent on Bedrock calls a lookup_policy tool. When the policy service throws, the handler catches the exception and returns a toolResult block with "is_error": true and the exception text, a pattern copied from the Anthropic API. boto3 rejects these follow-up requests with a parameter validation error on the tool result block. How should the handler signal the failure on Bedrock? A. Raise the exception out of the handler so the agent loop stops and the error is logged for an engineer. B. Return "status": "success" with an empty content list so Claude infers that the lookup found nothing. C. Set "status": "error" on the toolResult block and put the error message in its content list. D. Put the error text in a separate text part of the user message and omit the toolResult block.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: in the Converse API a toolResult block carries a status field whose value is success or error, with the error details supplied as text in content; there is no is_error field, so the Anthropic-API spelling fails validation. Returning an error status lets Claude read the message and often retry with corrected arguments. Option A terminates the whole conversation for a recoverable tool failure. Option B disguises a failure as an empty success, so Claude confidently reports that no policy exists. Option D leaves the toolUse block without a matching toolResult, which is itself a validation error, and strips the error of its association with the call. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • ToolResultBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Client-side tool use (AWS docs) • Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error

fields.Front: Your intake assistant's loop sends the initial request with a toolConfig containing three toolSpec definitions. After executing the requested tool it appends the assistant message and a user message holding the toolResult, then calls converse again with only modelId and messages. The second call fails 100% of the time with a validation error referencing the toolUse and toolResult content blocks. What is the fix? A. Strip the toolUse and toolResult blocks from the history before the follow-up call so the request contains only text. B. Move the tool results into the system parameter as text so they no longer count as tool content blocks in the messages. C. Replace the tool definitions with a note in the user message that lists the names of the tools Claude has already called. D. Pass the same toolConfig on every call in the loop, because a history that contains tool blocks requires the definitions.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: Converse requires toolConfig whenever the conversation contains toolUse or toolResult blocks, and Claude also needs the schemas to interpret the results it asked for, so the identical tool definitions must accompany every call in the loop, not just the first. Option A discards the tool call and result that the follow-up response depends on. Option B misuses the system prompt and breaks the pairing between a toolResult and its toolUseId. Option C describes tools in prose, which neither satisfies the API requirement nor gives Claude the schemas. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • Client-side tool use (AWS docs) • Converse API (AWS docs) — toolConfig • How tool use works — The agentic loop (client tools)

fields.Front: For the extraction step of your financial-services pipeline you want Claude to always call the extract_filing tool. Following an Anthropic API example, you set "toolChoice": {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_filing"} inside toolConfig, and boto3 rejects the request during parameter validation. Which toolChoice value is correct for the Converse API? A. {"any": {"name": "extract_filing"}} B. {"tool": {"name": "extract_filing"}} C. {"forced": {"tool": "extract_filing"}} D. {"toolChoice": "extract_filing"}
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: in Converse, toolChoice is an object keyed by mode, where {"auto": {}} lets Claude decide, {"any": {}} requires some tool, and {"tool": {"name": ...}} forces a specific tool, whereas the Anthropic API uses a type discriminator. Option A misuses the any mode, which takes an empty object and cannot name a tool, so even if accepted it would not guarantee extract_filing. Options C and D are not valid Converse shapes at all. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say some of the newest Claude models reject forced tool choice (any and tool) with a 400 error, including through Converse, and recommend auto with strict tool use or structured outputs on those models. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • ToolChoice — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Define tools — Forcing tool use • Anthropic Claude tool use (AWS docs) — Forced tool use

fields.Front: You are defining the get_claim_status tool for a Bedrock-based claims agent. Your first attempt places {"name": ..., "description": ..., "input_schema": {...}} directly in toolConfig.tools, and the request fails validation. How must each tool be declared in toolConfig? A. As a toolSpec object with name, description, and an inputSchema whose JSON Schema sits under a json key. B. As a function object with name, description, and parameters, matching the declaration style used by other providers. C. As a bare JSON Schema object whose title is used as the tool name and whose description doubles as the tool description. D. As a toolSpec object with name and description only; the argument schema is inferred from the tool's first use.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Converse wraps each tool in {"toolSpec": {"name": ..., "description": ..., "inputSchema": {"json": {...}}}}; the json wrapper and the camel-cased inputSchema are the Bedrock spelling of what the Anthropic API calls input_schema. Option B is another provider's format. Option C omits the explicit name and description that Claude relies on to choose and call the tool correctly. Option D is wrong because Claude never infers argument structure; the schema is what tells it which arguments to supply and with what types. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • ToolSpecification — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Client-side tool use (AWS docs) • Define tools — Specifying client tools

fields.Front: To cut sequential round trips, your claims agent on Bedrock adds a batch_tool whose toolSpec takes an invocations list, each entry holding a tool name and its arguments as a JSON-encoded string. The first test crashes in the handler with TypeError: argument after ** must be a mapping. With that line skipped so the test can continue, Bedrock rejects the follow-up request because the handler returned three toolResult blocks for the single batch_tool call. Which TWO changes make the handler work? (Select TWO.) A. Parse each invocation's arguments with json.loads before dispatching it through the existing run_tool function. B. Set toolChoice to the batch tool on every request so Claude always groups its calls into one invocation list. C. Rewrite the assistant message so that each invocation appears as its own toolUse block before sending the results. D. Collect the outputs of all invocations into one list and return them as a single toolResult bearing the batch call's toolUseId.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and D. Option A fixes the crash: the batch spec encodes arguments as a JSON string, so the handler must decode it into a dictionary before splatting it into the target tool, and delegating to the existing dispatcher keeps one implementation per tool. Option D fixes the rejection: from Bedrock's perspective there was exactly one toolUse (the batch call), so exactly one toolResult with its toolUseId must come back, containing the combined outputs. Option B forces the batch tool even for single-tool or no-tool turns and does nothing about the handler defects. Option C tampers with the model's own message, breaking the pairing between the real toolUse and its result. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • ToolResultBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Parallel tool use — Execution semantics • Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

fields.Front: Your healthcare intake assistant's chat() helper returns content[0]["text"] from every Converse response. Once tools were enabled, 9% of turns raise a KeyError; the logs show those responses begin with a toolUse part, and other turns silently lose text that appeared after the first part. How should the helper extract the reply text? A. Keep index 0 but wrap it in a try/except that returns an empty string whenever the first part has no text key. B. Instruct Claude in the system prompt to always begin its reply with a text part before any tool call. C. Collect the text values from every part that has a text key and join them, leaving tool parts to the tool handler. D. Set toolChoice to {"auto": {}} on every request so that responses are guaranteed to start with a text part.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: a Converse assistant message's content is a list of parts that may hold text, toolUse, and other part types in any order, so the helper should gather all text parts rather than assume position 0 is text. Option A hides the problem and returns nothing on the very turns where Claude included a tool call plus text. Option B relies on prompt compliance for a structural guarantee the API does not make. Option D is already the default and does not control part ordering. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • ContentBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Converse API (AWS docs) — Converse response • Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

fields.Front: You add Claude's built-in text editor tool to a Bedrock-based code-fixing agent by declaring the Anthropic-defined tool type and name for your Claude version in the request. Claude responds with tool-use requests such as {"command": "view", "path": "./handler.py"} and later str_replace, but no files are read or changed, and the run ends with Claude asking you for the file contents. What is missing? A. A hand-written JSON Schema describing each editor command, added to the tool definition next to its type and name. B. The contents of the files to be fixed, placed in the system prompt before the first request is sent. C. A switch to an MCP filesystem server that exposes the files, used in place of the built-in editor tool. D. A handler for each editor command that runs it against the files and returns the outcome as a tool result.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: for the text editor tool, only the tool's schema is built into Claude; the developer must implement a handler for each command that actually touches the file system and send each outcome back as a tool result. Without them, Claude's tool-use requests go unanswered, which is why it ends up asking for the file contents. Option A is wrong because the editor is a schema-less tool: its schema is built into the model and cannot be supplied or modified, so it is declared only by its Anthropic-defined type and name. Option B misunderstands the tool, whose purpose is to let Claude read and edit files it does not yet have in context; pasting the files into the prompt would still leave the edits unapplied and the tool-use requests unanswered. Option C swaps out the tool instead of supplying what is missing; the built-in editor supports edits as soon as the handlers exist. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • Text editor tool — Implement the text editor tool • Anthropic Claude tool use (AWS docs) — Anthropic defined tools • How tool use works — Anthropic-schema tools (client-executed)

fields.Front: In your claims agent the toolSpec names a tool get_current_datetime, while the dispatcher's run_tool function matches on the string get_current_date. Every attempt to use the tool raises the dispatcher's Unknown tool exception, and the model never 'corrects' the name no matter how the prompt is worded. What is the root cause, and what is the fix? A. Claude paraphrases tool names when prompts are informal; add the alternate spelling to the tool description so it learns the dispatcher's name. B. The dispatcher must match the toolSpec name exactly, since Claude emits the schema's name verbatim; fix the typo in the dispatcher. C. Bedrock normalizes tool names by dropping trailing words such as time; register the tool under the shortened name instead. D. Return an error toolResult for the unknown name so Claude retries with the spelling the dispatcher expects.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: the name in a toolUse part is always the exact string declared in the toolSpec, so a mismatch between schema and dispatcher is a developer typo, and the dispatcher's key must be corrected to match the schema. Option A asks the model to work around your bug and is impossible anyway, since Claude can only call declared names. Option C invents behavior that Bedrock does not have. Option D cannot succeed because the only name Claude knows is the declared one; the loop would simply repeat the error. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • ToolUseBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Client-side tool use (AWS docs) • Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

fields.Front: Your underwriting team extracts policy_number, date_of_loss, claim_amount, and claimant from claims letters on Bedrock. Today the pipeline asks for JSON in the reply text and parses it, which fails on 4% of letters. A teammate proposes switching to a single flexible toJSON tool whose input schema accepts any properties, with the wanted fields listed only in the prompt. The extracted values feed payment decisions. Which TWO design choices best fit this pipeline? (Select TWO.) A. Keep the prompt-based JSON approach and add a code-block prefill plus a stopSequences entry in inferenceConfig. B. Define a dedicated toolSpec whose inputSchema mirrors the four fields and read them from the returned toolUse input. C. Prefer a dedicated schema over the flexible toJSON tool for this task, reserving the flexible tool for lower-stakes extractions. D. Keep the prompt-based JSON approach and re-send any letter whose reply fails to parse until it returns valid JSON.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B and C. Option B replaces text parsing with tool-based extraction: Claude 'calls' a tool whose inputs are the desired structure, so the four fields arrive as structured arguments shaped by the schema rather than as free text that must be parsed. Option C applies the trade-off between the two tool-based styles: a flexible toJSON tool is convenient for rapidly changing or low-stakes structures but yields somewhat lower-quality results, so a critical financial extraction warrants a dedicated schema. Option A keeps the fragile text-parsing path; a prefill and stop sequence only make the JSON easier to locate in the reply and add none of the structure a tool call provides. Option D retries the same fragile path: re-sending adds cost and delay, and a reply that finally parses has still not been checked against any schema, so the four fields can be missing or malformed. Currency note (Oct 2026): prefilled assistant messages are no longer supported on Claude 4.6 and later models (the request returns a 400 error), and strict tool use can now guarantee that tool inputs match the schema. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Tool use course — Forcing JSON with tool use (anthropics/courses, GitHub) • Strict tool use • Prompting best practices — Migrating away from prefilled responses

fields.Front: Your document intake system extracts a different set of fields for each of 14 internal form types, and the field lists change monthly. The team maintains 14 hand-written toolSpec schemas and estimates 6 hours of schema edits per change cycle; none of the 14 outputs is used for regulated decisions. Which approach best reduces maintenance while keeping extraction reliable? A. Register one flexible toJSON tool with an open object input and list each form type's properties and types in the prompt. B. Merge the 14 schemas into a single toolSpec with every possible field marked optional so that one schema covers all of the forms. C. Add a routing classifier that inspects each document and selects which of the 14 toolSpec schemas to send with the request. D. Return to prompt-based JSON extraction with a code-block prefill and stop sequence so that no schemas are needed at all.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is the flexible extraction pattern: a single toJSON tool whose input accepts arbitrary properties, with the desired structure written in the prompt, so changing a form's fields means editing prompt text rather than a schema. The trade-off is slightly lower fidelity than a dedicated schema, which is acceptable here because no output drives regulated decisions. Option B produces a sprawling schema in which Claude must guess which of dozens of optional fields apply to each form. Option C adds a classifier to solve a maintenance problem and still leaves 14 schemas to maintain. Option D gives up the reliability of tool-based extraction entirely. Currency note (Oct 2026): prefilled assistant messages are no longer supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, so option D's technique is rejected outright on current models. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Tool use course — Forcing JSON with tool use (anthropics/courses, GitHub) • Define tools — Specifying client tools • Prompting best practices — Migrating away from prefilled responses

fields.Front: Your claims pipeline on Bedrock extracts adjuster_name from intake emails with a flexible toJSON tool: its input schema accepts any properties, and the prompt lists the fields to return. 18% of emails name no adjuster; in those cases Claude sometimes omits the key, sometimes returns an empty string, and in 3% of cases supplies a name found elsewhere in the email signature. Downstream code treats any string as a valid assignment. What is the most effective change? A. Mark adjuster_name as required in the toJSON tool's inputSchema so that Claude must always supply a value for it on every email. B. Lower the temperature to 0 so that the behavior for emails with no adjuster becomes consistent and repeatable from run to run. C. Run a second extraction call for each email and accept the adjuster name only when both calls return exactly the same string. D. Say in the prompt's field list that adjuster_name must be null when no adjuster is named, and route null to manual assignment.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: with the flexible tool the schema is deliberately open, so the rules for each property, including what to do when the source lacks it, live in the prompt's field list; an explicit null convention gives downstream code an unambiguous signal instead of an absent key, an empty string, or a fabricated name. Option A cannot express the absent case; requiring the field pushes Claude toward inventing a value. Option B makes the output more repeatable but does not define what the correct output is. Option C doubles cost and still has no rule for the missing case, so both calls can agree on the same fabricated name. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • Define tools — Specifying client tools

fields.Front: After switching your filing extractor to a forced extract_filing tool on Bedrock, the post-processing step calls json.loads(part["toolUse"]["input"]) and every run fails with TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not dict. What should the pipeline do with the tool input? A. Call json.dumps on the input first so that json.loads can then re-parse the string into a clean dictionary. B. Switch back to prompt-based extraction, since tool inputs cannot be read as JSON when they come through the Converse API. C. Use part["toolUse"]["input"] as it is, because Converse returns the arguments already parsed into a dictionary. D. Retry the request with a higher maxTokens so that the tool input arrives complete and json.loads can parse it.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: in a Converse response the toolUse part's input is already a dictionary matching the tool's inputSchema, so the extracted values can be used as-is; the pipeline's parse step is redundant and is exactly what fails. Option A round-trips the data through a string for no reason. Option B abandons the more reliable extraction path over a misunderstanding of the response shape. Option D addresses truncation, which is not occurring; the error is a client-side type error. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • ToolUseBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Client-side tool use (AWS docs) • Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

fields.Front:
Your nightly Bedrock job extracts fields from about 9,000 claims letters. When extraction of any single letter fails validation (a missing required field or an unparseable date), the job raises and the entire run stops; on 3 of the last 5 nights, one bad letter delayed all 9,000 by a day.

How should the job handle a failed extraction?

A. Catch the validation error, write whatever fields were extracted for that letter, and continue with the rest.
B. Retry the failing letter up to five times with exponential backoff, log each attempt, and halt the run if the last retry fails.
C. Log the letter ID, the failing field and the reason, route that letter to a review queue, and continue with the rest.
D. Wrap the batch in one database transaction, roll it back when a letter fails validation, and alert the on-call engineer.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: one document's failure is an independent, recoverable event, so the job should capture structured error context (which letter, which field, why) that a reviewer can act on and keep processing the other letters. Option A silently passes unvalidated data into downstream systems. Option B still halts the run for a letter that may be genuinely unextractable, and blind retries of a deterministic validation failure rarely help. Option D maximizes the blast radius of a single failure, which is the current problem. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Batch processing — Retrieving batch results • View the results of a batch inference job (AWS docs)

fields.Front: Claims arrive as PDFs. Your pipeline runs a separate OCR service, then sends the recovered text to Claude through the Bedrock Converse API for field extraction. OCR errors account for 7% of wrong field values, and the OCR step adds 40 seconds per document. What is the most direct simplification? A. Keep the OCR step but add few-shot examples of common OCR misreads to the extraction prompt so that Claude corrects them. B. Send each PDF as a document part with citations enabled, next to the instruction, and remove the OCR step. C. Convert each PDF page to an image and send up to 20 image parts per request for Claude to transcribe before extracting. D. Add a second Claude call that cleans up the OCR output before the extraction call sees it, catching the common misreads.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Claude accepts the PDF itself as a document content part alongside the text prompt, and through Converse, enabling citations on that part is what gives Claude the full visual reading of each page (without it, Converse applies only basic text extraction and cannot analyze images or layouts), so the OCR service, its misreads and its 40 seconds leave the pipeline in one change. Option A keeps the flawed step and tries to prompt around its output. Option C reintroduces a conversion step and treats the PDF as a stack of images when native document input exists. Option D adds a second model call to clean up a step that can simply be removed. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • PDF support — Amazon Bedrock PDF support • DocumentBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Claude on Amazon Bedrock (Opus 4.6 and earlier) — PDF support on Bedrock

fields.Front:
Your insurance knowledge base uses hybrid retrieval (a vector index plus a BM25 index, merged with rank fusion). An audit of 400 adjuster questions shows the correct section is retrieved in 91% of cases but ranks second or third in 35% of them, and the prompt budget allows only the top result to be included.

Which change most directly improves the rank of the correct section?

A. Add a reranking step in which Claude reads the query and the merged candidates and reorders them by relevance.
B. Increase the retrieval depth so that the top ten candidates are all placed in the prompt for the answer step to sort out.
C. Re-chunk the corpus with a larger overlap so that neighboring sections share more text and rank closer together.
D. Replace the embedding model with one that produces larger vectors, then re-embed the corpus and rebuild the vector index.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the failure is ordering among already-retrieved candidates, which is exactly what an LLM reranker fixes: a post-processing call that reads the query and each candidate and returns them in decreasing relevance, at the cost of one extra model call's latency. Option B violates the stated prompt budget and pushes the ranking problem onto the answer step. Option C changes what is retrieved, not how candidates are ordered, and recall is already 91%. Option D is a speculative, expensive change with no evidence that embedding quality is the bottleneck. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic Engineering) — Further boosting performance with Reranking • Enhancing RAG with contextual retrieval (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
After adding a Claude reranker to your claims knowledge base, answer accuracy rose from 78% to 90%, but p50 latency grew by 4 seconds. Profiling shows the reranker receives all 40 merged candidates and is asked to return the reordered chunks' full text, which averages 3,000 output tokens per query.

Which TWO changes cut the reranking latency while preserving most of the accuracy gain? (Select TWO.)

A. Give each candidate a short temporary ID and have the reranker return only the ordered IDs, mapping them back to text in code.
B. Pass only the top 10 merged candidates to the reranker instead of all 40, which shrinks the prompt it has to read.
C. Skip the reranker whenever the top two rank-fusion scores differ by more than 0.1, since the leader is then clear.
D. Drop the BM25 index so that the merge step produces fewer candidates for the reranker to read on each query.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and B. Option A removes the dominant cost: having Claude copy chunk text back is slow and wasteful, whereas returning an ordered list of IDs takes a handful of tokens and lets code look up the text. Option B shrinks the reranker's input to the candidates that could plausibly be top-ranked, cutting input tokens without discarding the ordering benefit. Option C uses a score gap as a confidence proxy, but rank-fusion scores are coarse and the failures reranking fixes are precisely the cases where a wrong candidate leads; it silently skips the fix. Option D reduces recall for exact-term queries to save a small amount of reranker input. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic Engineering) — Cost and latency considerations • Reducing latency — Optimize prompt and output length • Enhancing RAG with contextual retrieval (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
Your financial-services research assistant chunks 80-page reports by section. Chunks refer to 'the incident' or 'the program' without naming them, since the names appear only in each report's introduction. Queries that name the incident retrieve the introduction but miss the sections that actually discuss it; recall on such queries is 58%.

Which change best addresses the failure?

A. Add a reranking step so that the sections discussing the incident move above the introduction in the merged list of results.
B. Increase chunk overlap so that each section includes the tail of the previous section and inherits some of its wording.
C. Add few-shot examples to the answer prompt showing how to interpret unnamed references such as 'the incident' or 'the program'.
D. Before indexing, have Claude write a short context situating each chunk in its report, and index the chunk with it prepended.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is contextual retrieval: chunking strips each section of document-level context, and a preprocessing step that asks Claude to situate the chunk within the source document restores references such as the incident's name into the text that gets embedded and indexed, so queries naming it can match. Option A can only reorder candidates that were retrieved, and the missing sections are not being retrieved at all. Option B adds neighboring text, not the introduction's naming context that lives far away in the document. Option C acts at answer time, after retrieval has already failed. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic Engineering) — Introducing Contextual Retrieval • Enhancing RAG with contextual retrieval (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
You are applying contextual retrieval to 400-page regulatory filings. The contextualization prompt is supposed to include the full source document with each chunk, but the filings are far too large for that, and the per-chunk cost would be prohibitive even where they fit.

How should the context-generation prompt be built for each chunk?

A. Send only the chunk itself and ask Claude to infer the document's context from the chunk's own wording and terminology.
B. Send a random sample of 20 chunks drawn from across the filing along with the target chunk to stand in for the whole.
C. Send the filing's opening chunks plus the chunks just before the target chunk, leaving out the middle of the document.
D. Switch to the largest available model so that the full filing fits in the context window for every chunk's prompt.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is the practical strategy for oversized sources: the document's opening chunks usually carry the summary or abstract that explains what the whole document is about, and the chunks just before the target supply its local context, while distant middle sections add little; this keeps each prompt small and cheap. Option A defeats the purpose, since the chunk alone lacks the context being added. Option B supplies unrelated material at random and may omit the introduction entirely. Option D attacks the problem with a bigger context window at far higher cost and does nothing for the per-chunk cost concern. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic Engineering) — Implementing Contextual Retrieval • Enhancing RAG with contextual retrieval (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front: Your team adopted contextual retrieval for its claims knowledge base and re-embedded every chunk with its generated context, but left the BM25 index built from the raw chunks. Semantic queries improved, yet keyword queries containing a report code that appears only in the generated context (for example INC-2023-Q4-011) still miss the relevant sections. What is the cause? A. BM25 cannot match hyphenated codes such as this one; the tokenizer must be replaced before the added context can help. B. The contextualized chunk must go into both the vector index and the BM25 index; the lexical index still holds the raw text. C. The generated context is too short to shift the BM25 term weights; regenerate it with a larger model and longer output. D. Reciprocal Rank Fusion ignores BM25 results whenever the vector index returns a strong match, so lexical hits are dropped.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: contextual retrieval works by indexing the contextualized chunk (generated context plus original text) in every search path, the vector index and the BM25 index alike. Because the lexical index was left with raw chunks, the report code exists only in the embedded text, so exact-term queries cannot find it. Option A blames tokenization when the term is simply absent from the index. Option C misdiagnoses; a term that is not in the indexed text has no weight regardless of context length. Option D misstates rank fusion, which sums contributions from every list. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic Engineering) — Introducing Contextual Retrieval • Enhancing RAG with contextual retrieval (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
Your document-intake search currently calls the vector index and the BM25 index directly from the request handler, with the merge logic written inline. The team now wants to add a third search method (a title-and-metadata index), and a later proposal calls for a fourth. Each addition currently requires rewriting the handler and its merge code.

Which design best accommodates additional search methods?

A. Run the methods as a pipeline in which each search is restricted to the results returned by the previous method.
B. Benchmark the three methods on sample queries, keep the best-scoring one, and retire the other two methods.
C. Leave the handler's inline merge logic untouched and append each new index's results after the merged list.
D. Put the indexes behind one retriever with a shared search interface that queries each and merges the ranked lists.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the modular multi-search design: because every index implements the same small API, a Retriever wrapper can forward add_document and search to each, collect the ranked lists, and merge them with rank fusion, so adding a fourth method means adding one class rather than rewriting the handler. Option A turns parallel, complementary searches into a cascade in which the first method's misses can never be recovered. Option B abandons multi-method search: retiring the other methods throws away the semantic, lexical or metadata coverage each one adds, and nothing in it makes a fourth method easier to add. Option C bypasses the merge, so the new index's results always sit below the others whatever their relevance, and the fourth method would need the same special case again. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic Engineering) — A primer on RAG: scaling to larger knowledge bases • Enhancing RAG with contextual retrieval (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
An engineer reports a suspected bug in your hybrid claims search: a section ranked first by the vector index but absent from the BM25 results is consistently outranked in the merged list by a section ranked second in both indexes. The pipeline merges with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, summing 1/(1 + rank) across the indexes.

How should you respond?

A. Explain that this is correct: second place in both indexes scores 1/3 + 1/3, which beats the 1/2 earned by first place in only one.
B. Confirm the bug: the top vector result should always win, so the vector index's ranks need a higher weight in the merge than the BM25 ranks.
C. Fix the merge so that a section missing from one index receives that index's rank 1 instead of contributing nothing to its score.
D. Replace the fusion step with the raw cosine distance from the vector index so that ties and near-ties are broken numerically.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: under Reciprocal Rank Fusion each index contributes 1/(1 + rank) for the documents it returned and nothing for those it did not, so a section that both methods rank highly accumulates more score than one that only a single method favors; this consensus effect is the intended behavior of hybrid search. Option B would reintroduce the single-method blind spots that hybrid search exists to fix. Option C rewards absence from an index, inverting the meaning of the score. Option D discards the lexical signal entirely and compares quantities that are not on the same scale. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic Engineering) — A primer on RAG: scaling to larger knowledge bases • Enhancing RAG with contextual retrieval (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
Your healthcare knowledge base was indexed with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2. A later refactor moved query embedding into a shared service that uses a different embedding model. Retrieval quality collapsed: cosine distances for obviously relevant chunks now cluster near 1.0, and the top results look random.

What is the root cause?

A. The shared service's embedding model is less accurate than Titan V2 on healthcare text and ranks the chunks worse.
B. The query service embeds queries with a different model than the one that produced the stored chunk vectors.
C. The refactor dropped the client-side step that re-normalizes Titan V2 vectors before cosine distance is computed.
D. The new shared service stopped querying the BM25 index that used to run alongside the vector index.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: semantic search compares the query embedding with stored chunk embeddings, which only makes sense when both come from the same model, since each model defines its own vector space; embedding queries with a different model produces near-random similarities. Option A blames the new model's accuracy, but accuracy is not what failed: vectors from different models are not comparable however good each model is, so mixing them gives results that look random rather than merely worse. Option C is wrong on the facts, since cosine distance depends on the angle between two vectors and not on their length, and it would not explain a collapse that coincided with the model change. Option D concerns lexical search and cannot make correct vector matches disappear. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Embeddings — Quickstart example • How Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases work (AWS docs)

fields.Front:
Your Bedrock claims extraction prompt scores 9.1 out of 10 on an eval set of 60 synthetic claim letters generated by Claude, yet adjusters report that 15% of real letters, which carry handwritten annotations, scanned tables, and non-standard layouts, yield wrong field values.

How should the eval dataset be rebuilt?

A. Generate 500 synthetic letters instead of 60 and instruct the generator to include unusual layouts, annotations, and scanned tables.
B. Use the pipeline's own production outputs as the expected values so that the eval reflects the real documents it processes.
C. Replace the dataset with a model grader that judges each production output on its own merits, without any expected values.
D. Sample real claim letters from production, have adjusters label each field's expected value, and store each letter with its labels.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: an eval dataset must contain inputs representative of what the prompt sees in production, and for extraction each case needs a trustworthy expected output; sampling real letters and having domain experts label the expected field values provides both. Option A scales up synthetic data that has already proven unrepresentative of production quirks. Option B is circular, since the pipeline's outputs are what is suspected to be wrong. Option C drops ground truth entirely, so the eval could not detect the wrong values that adjusters are reporting. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Eval design principles • Building evals (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front: Your document-intake eval has 300 labeled test cases, each with the expected policy_number, claim_amount, and date_of_loss. Today a Sonnet model grader reads each output and the expected values and assigns a 1 to 10 score; the grading calls cost more than the extraction itself, and spot checks find the grader awarding 8 out of 10 to outputs with a wrong claim amount. How should grading be changed for these fields? A. Keep the model grader but ask it to list strengths and weaknesses before the score so that it grades more strictly and consistently. B. Switch to human grading for all 300 cases on every run to guarantee that wrong claim amounts are caught before each release. C. Grade these fields in code by comparing each normalized value with its expected value, and keep model grading for free-text fields. D. Raise the grader's temperature so that its scores spread across the full 1 to 10 range instead of clustering near the middle.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: when a test case carries expected values, a code grader can compare each extracted field exactly (after normalizing dates and currency formats), which is deterministic, cheap, and cannot award partial credit to a wrong amount; model graders earn their cost on judgments code cannot make, such as the quality of a free-text summary. Option A improves a model grader's calibration but still applies a subjective judge to an objective comparison. Option B is accurate but far too slow and tedious to run on every iteration. Option D adds randomness to a grader whose problem is leniency, not lack of spread. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Grade your evaluations • Building evals (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
Your Bedrock eval covers 120 varied intake tasks (summaries, coded lists, form-letter drafts). The model grader receives the task, the output, and a single general rubric, and its scores cluster between 6 and 7 regardless of whether the specific task was accomplished; reviewers find that the grader's reasoning rarely mentions task-specific requirements.

What change most improves the grader's ability to separate good outputs from bad ones?

A. Generate solution criteria for each test case when the dataset is built and add them to the grader prompt.
B. Have the grader return just a numeric score, without written reasoning, for each of the 120 tasks in the eval.
C. Grow the dataset from 120 to 1,200 tasks, adding more cases of each task type, and rerun the grader on the set.
D. Switch to a larger grader model and keep the single general rubric in the grader prompt for the 120 tasks.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: when tasks vary widely, a general rubric cannot tell the grader what success means for each one, so the dataset generator should emit per-case solution criteria alongside the task, and the grader prompt should include them next to the output being judged. Option B removes the reasoning that helps a grader commit to a concrete score and makes middling scores more likely, not less. Option C makes an uninformative signal more precise without making it informative. Option D asks a bigger model to guess requirements that could simply be provided. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Tips for LLM-based grading • Building evals (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front:
Your team runs a prompt eval on Bedrock after every change to the claims summarization prompt and records only the average score. The last change moved the average from 7.4 to 6.9, and nobody can say which test cases regressed or why, so the change was reverted blindly.

What should each eval run record?

A. The grader's score for each test case and the aggregate score, with the run date and the prompt version.
B. The input, raw output, grader's score and grader's reasoning for each test case, plus the aggregate score.
C. The aggregate score, the full prompt text of each run, and a diff of the prompt against the previous run.
D. The aggregate score, plus a short human-written summary of what changed in the outputs between runs.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: a sound eval pipeline assembles a result per test case containing the output, the test case, the score, and the grader's reasoning, and it is that per-case record (rendered into a report) that lets engineers see which inputs regressed and what the grader objected to. Option A keeps numbers without the evidence needed to interpret them. Option C explains what changed in the prompt but not how the outputs changed. Option D is unreproducible and depends on someone having already done the analysis the pipeline should enable. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Tips for LLM-based grading • Building evals (Claude Cookbook)

fields.Front: For complex coverage-dispute analyses in your claims pipeline, evals show that enabling extended thinking is warranted. A developer adds thinking=True and budget_tokens=2048 as keyword arguments to the boto3 converse call, and boto3 rejects the call with a parameter validation error. How is extended thinking enabled through the Converse API? A. By passing additionalModelRequestFields={"thinking": {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 2048}} to converse. B. By adding {"thinking": true} to inferenceConfig alongside temperature and maxTokens. C. By appending a reasoningContent part to the last user message to request reasoning for that turn. D. By prefixing the user prompt with a directive to think step by step; Bedrock offers no API setting for it.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Converse models the common parameters natively, and model-specific features such as Anthropic's extended thinking are passed through additionalModelRequestFields, where the thinking object enables the feature and sets budget_tokens (which must be at least 1,024). Option B places the setting in inferenceConfig, which accepts only Converse's standard sampling fields. Option C confuses a response part type with a request parameter. Option D is chain-of-thought prompting, a different technique that produces neither the separate reasoning part nor the budget control. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say this manual form (type enabled with budget_tokens) is deprecated on Claude 4.6 models and rejected with a 400 error by Claude 4.7 and later models, which use adaptive thinking instead. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Use Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet's reasoning capability on Amazon Bedrock (AWS docs) • Converse API (AWS docs) — Additional model request fields • Extended thinking — Migrating to adaptive thinking

fields.Front: Your healthcare intake assistant on Bedrock runs with extended thinking and calls tools, and it stores every message of a conversation in a database. To save space, the storage layer truncates each reasoningContent part's text to 500 characters. When a tool result is sent back together with the stored assistant message that requested the tool, Bedrock rejects the request with an error about the reasoning signature; some stored assistant messages also contain a part holding only redactedContent, which the team planned to drop. How should reasoning parts be handled when a tool result is sent back? A. Truncate the text in each reasoningContent part as planned and recompute its signature locally for the shortened text. B. Convert each reasoningContent part into a plain text part that carries the same reasoning text word for word. C. Store and resend each reasoningContent part exactly as received, whether it holds signed text or redactedContent. D. Drop each reasoningContent part, including parts that hold just redactedContent, from the stored assistant message.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: the signature on a reasoningContent part is a cryptographic token that lets Claude verify the reasoning text was not modified, so any edit, including truncation, invalidates it; redactedContent is reasoning in encrypted form, provided precisely so it can be returned to Claude without losing context. When a tool result is returned, the reasoning parts of the assistant message that requested the tool must come back complete and unmodified. Option A is impossible; the signature is not something your code can generate. Option B strips the signature and presents the reasoning as ordinary assistant text, altering the conversation. Option D removes reasoning that a tool-use turn is required to carry and discards the context that the redacted form exists to preserve. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • ReasoningContentBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Thinking — Preserving thinking blocks • Extended thinking (AWS docs) — Preserving thinking blocks

fields.Front: Your claims agent on Bedrock sends a 6,000-token system prompt and 1,200 tokens of tool schemas on every request, with a cachePoint after the system prompt. The usage field shows a full-prefix cacheWriteInputTokens value on every request and cacheReadInputTokens of 0, even for requests two seconds apart. The system prompt begins with a line such as Current time: 2026-08-26T09:14:05Z, refreshed on every request. Why is the cache never read, and what is the fix? A. The five-minute cache lifetime is too short for this traffic pattern; increase the request rate so that cache entries never expire. B. The system prompt exceeds the maximum size for caching; split it into two parts of fewer than 1,024 tokens each with their own cache points. C. Tool schemas cannot be cached on Bedrock, and their presence in the request invalidates the system prompt's cache entry on every call. D. The timestamp changes the content before the cache point on every request; move it below the cache point (for example, into the user message).
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: a cache read requires that everything before the cachePoint be identical to a previous request within the cache lifetime; a per-request timestamp at the top of the system prompt guarantees a mismatch, so every request is a fresh write. Moving dynamic content after the cache point preserves the stable prefix. Option A misreads the evidence, since the requests are seconds apart, well inside the lifetime. Option B has the threshold backwards: a prefix must reach a minimum token count before it can be cached (1,024 on many models; the figure depends on the model), and the usage data shows this prefix being written to the cache on every request, so its size is not the obstacle. Option C is false; tool definition lists are one of the most common places to put a cache point. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Prompt caching for faster model inference (AWS docs) — Explicit Prompt Caching • Prompt caching — How automatic prefix checking works • TokenUsage — Converse API reference (AWS docs)

fields.Front: Your healthcare intake assistant passes a patient-instructions PDF as a document part with citations enabled and renders content[0]["text"] from the response. Clinicians see fluent answers but no source markers, and the compliance team cannot verify which page supports each statement, even though citations were 'turned on'. What is the correct way to render the response? A. Loop over every part of the response content, rendering text parts as text and citationsContent parts with their cited passage and page. B. Ask Claude in the prompt to append page numbers in brackets after each sentence instead of relying on the citations feature to supply them. C. Enable citations on the user text part as well as the document part, since source markers only appear when both parts have it enabled. D. Increase maxTokens, since citation markers are emitted at the very end of the response and are being cut off by the output limit.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: with citations enabled, the Converse response interleaves ordinary text parts with citationsContent parts, each holding generated text together with the citations that support it (the cited passage and where in the document it came from); reading only the first part discards every citation and the text that follows it. Option B abandons verifiable citations for model-authored page numbers that cannot be trusted. Option C invents a requirement; citations are enabled on the document part. Option D is wrong on mechanics, since citations travel in their own parts next to the text they support, not in a trailer that gets truncated. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • CitationsContentBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • DocumentBlock — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Citations — How citations work

fields.Front: Your platform team installs Claude Code for engineers who may only use models through your organization's AWS Bedrock account. On first run, Claude Code shows its login prompt and, when an engineer signs in with a personal Anthropic account, sends every request to Anthropic's API instead of Bedrock. What configuration makes Claude Code use Bedrock? A. Add an MCP server to Claude Code that proxies its model requests to the Bedrock endpoint in your organization's account. B. Paste the Bedrock inference profile ID into the login prompt in place of an API key so that requests are routed to Bedrock. C. Set the CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK environment variable, plus region and model settings, so that Claude Code calls Bedrock. D. Run init inside a repository that already contains boto3 Bedrock code so that Claude Code detects the provider from the project.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: by default Claude Code targets the Anthropic API, and the scripted setup for Bedrock is to set a small number of environment variables, the Bedrock switch plus region and model configuration, after which Claude Code authenticates with your AWS credentials rather than an Anthropic key. Option A misuses MCP, which adds tools to Claude Code and has nothing to do with which model endpoint it calls. Option B puts a routing identifier where a credential is expected. Option D confuses init, which scans a codebase to write CLAUDE.md, with provider configuration. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock — 3. Configure Claude Code • Environment variables (Claude Code Docs)

fields.Front: Your team wires a daily GitHub Action in which Claude Code pulls the last 24 hours of CloudWatch errors from the production claims app (deduplicated to a manageable set), diagnoses each, and applies a fix. In the first version the Action commits directly to main and deploys. After two weeks, one automated fix changed a Bedrock model ID to one that is not enabled in production, and it reached users before anyone noticed. What change most improves the workflow? A. Have the Action open a pull request against main with Claude's explanation of each fix, for human review and merge. B. Restrict the Action to errors that have recurred at least 50 times in the logs before it attempts a fix. C. Add a second Claude call that reviews the first call's fix and commits the change once the reviewer approves it. D. Limit the Action to editing files under src/handlers/ and keep the configuration files out of its reach.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the agent should explain and propose fixes through a pull request that a human reviews before merge; automated debugging still requires human review of proposed changes, and a PR preserves the speed of automated diagnosis while keeping a person accountable for what ships. Option B changes which errors get attention, not whether a bad fix can deploy. Option C substitutes one model's judgment for another's on a change with production impact, without human accountability. Option D is a brittle path restriction that would also block legitimate fixes, and many bad fixes live inside handler code anyway. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Building effective agents (Anthropic Engineering) — B. Coding agents • Claude Code GitHub Actions — Interactive and automation modes

fields.Front:
Your company wants to build its first autonomous agent on Bedrock. Three candidates are proposed: (1) an agent that writes and runs unit tests for the claims codebase and opens PRs; (2) an agent that approves and issues claim payments up to $50,000 without review; (3) an agent that answers rare, low-value FAQ lookups. Each would loop over a small, focused toolset and inspect its environment through tool calls.

Which candidate best matches the qualities of a good first agent, and why?

A. Candidate 2, because the highest-value task justifies the investment in an agent, its tooling, and its evaluation suite.
B. Candidate 3, because a low-stakes task is the safest possible place to learn how agents behave in production before scaling up.
C. Candidate 2, provided the agent reports a confidence score and any payment below 0.8 confidence is held for review.
D. Candidate 1, because the work is high value while a mistaken edit is cheap to catch in review and tests before it does harm.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: agents suit high-value tasks where failures do not cause large economic or safety damage; writing code is valuable, and a bad change is recoverable through review and tests. Option A picks value while ignoring the unbounded cost of an autonomous payment error. Option B is safe but so low in value that the effort of building and evaluating an agent is not justified. Option C tries to make the risky candidate acceptable with a self-reported confidence gate, which is not a reliable control. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Building effective agents (Anthropic Engineering) — Agents • Building effective agents (Anthropic Engineering) — B. Coding agents

fields.Front: A claims agent your team runs on Bedrock declares two tools. get_current_datetime is described as "Returns date and time information." and get_filing_deadline as "Returns date information for a claim." The agent's dispatcher function, run_tool, has an entry for each declared name, and its Unknown tool exception has not fired in 4,000 logged calls: each call ran the function registered under the name Claude emitted. When policyholders ask how long they have left to file, 31% of conversations show Claude calling get_current_datetime and adding 30 days to the loss date, which is wrong for policies with a 60-day window. What is the root cause, and what is the fix? A. The dispatcher maps each name to a single function; add a branch that reroutes deadline questions from get_current_datetime to get_filing_deadline. B. The handler answers calls that do not fit the question; make get_current_datetime return an error result whenever a claim is being discussed. C. The two descriptions do not say what separates the tools; rewrite them to state what get_filing_deadline returns and when to call each tool. D. The system prompt has no examples of deadline questions; add six sample conversations that end in a call to get_filing_deadline.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The logs rule out the code: each call named a declared tool and ran the function registered for it, so the dispatcher did what Claude asked. What went wrong is the choice of tool, and tool descriptions are the main basis Claude has for that choice. Two one-line descriptions that both promise "date information" give it nothing to tell the clock from the claim-specific deadline, so option C rewrites them to say what each tool returns and when to call it. Option A patches the dispatcher, which receives a tool name and arguments, not the policyholder's question, and so has nothing to reroute on. Option B turns a correct result into an error: the handler cannot tell which calls were misplaced, and each one would cost an extra round trip. Option D adds examples and token overhead to the prompt while the ambiguous descriptions stay in place. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • Define tools — Best practices for tool definitions • Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

fields.Front: The extraction step of a financial-services pipeline your team runs on Bedrock sends Claude one document per request with two tools. extract_filing is described as "Extracts data from a filing." and extract_exhibit as "Extracts data from an exhibit." Annual reports, which themselves refer to many agreements, belong with the first tool. The contracts attached to them, such as credit agreements, belong with the second, whose schema has fields for the parties and the term. Each response contains exactly one tool call, yet 17% of credit agreements go to extract_filing and come back with most fields empty. Which change addresses these errors? A. Set toolChoice to {"tool": {"name": "extract_filing"}} on each request that the extraction step sends. B. Set toolChoice to {"any": {}} on each request, in place of the default value of {"auto": {}}. C. Add a system prompt rule that routes a document containing the word "agreement" to extract_exhibit. D. Rewrite the two descriptions to say which documents extract_filing and extract_exhibit each handle.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Each response already contains one tool call, so the errors lie in which tool Claude picks, and that choice rests on the tool descriptions. Two one-line descriptions that never say what counts as a filing or an exhibit leave a credit agreement that arrives with an annual report open to either reading, so option D spells out which documents each tool handles and where the boundary lies. Option A forces extract_filing for every document, which sends every exhibit to the wrong schema. Option B only requires that some tool be called, which is already the case, and leaves the choice between the two untouched. Option C ties routing to a keyword that annual reports contain as well, so it would misroute filings in the other direction. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say the newest Claude models reject forced tool choice (any or a named tool) with a 400 error. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • Define tools — Best practices for tool definitions • ToolChoice — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • Define tools — Forcing tool use

fields.Front: A claims intake assistant your team runs on Bedrock has to confirm the caller's policy before it does anything else. To make sure of that, its loop sends each request with one toolConfig: three toolSpec definitions (verify_policy, lookup_claim and open_claim) and a toolChoice that names verify_policy. After executing the requested tool, the loop appends the assistant message and a user message holding the toolResult, then calls converse with the identical configuration. In testing, each response is one more verify_policy call, and the loop stops at its limit of 10 calls without a claim lookup or a reply to the caller. What is the fix? A. Name verify_policy in toolChoice on the first call, and send {"auto": {}} with the same tools after it. B. Keep the identical toolConfig on each call, and raise the limit of the loop from 10 calls to 25 calls. C. Send toolConfig on the first call, and leave it out of the later calls that carry a toolResult. D. Keep the identical toolConfig on each call, and tell Claude in the system prompt to verify once.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. A toolChoice that names a tool makes Claude call that tool on that request, whatever the conversation already contains. Because the loop resends the identical configuration, every response is a verify_policy call and the stop reason never changes, so the loop ends only at its cap. Option A forces on the first call alone, which guarantees that verification runs first, and its later calls use auto with the same tools so that Claude can look up the claim, open one and reply. Option B gives the same forced call more repetitions. Option D relies on an instruction that the forced choice overrides on every request. Option C withdraws the tool definitions from exactly the calls that need the other two tools. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say the newest Claude models reject forced tool choice (any or a named tool) with a 400 error and recommend auto with strict tool use on those models. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • Define tools — Forcing tool use • ToolChoice — Converse API reference (AWS docs) • How tool use works — The agentic loop (client tools)

fields.Front: A healthcare intake assistant your team runs on Bedrock answers patients through a chat() helper. Each Converse request carries two tools, lookup_appointment and reschedule_appointment, and a toolChoice of {"any": {}}, which was set after the assistant once answered a scheduling question from memory. The helper joins the text of every text part into the reply shown to the patient. On the 9% of turns that need no lookup, such as a patient saying thanks or asking for the clinic's phone number given in the system prompt, the response holds a toolUse part with made-up arguments and no text part, so the patient sees an empty reply. How should the requests be changed? A. Keep {"any": {}} and expand both tool descriptions to say when a tool is not to be called. B. Send {"auto": {}} and state in the system prompt which kinds of question need a lookup first. C. Keep {"any": {}} and have the helper take the reply from the first part with a text key. D. Send {"tool": {"name": "lookup_appointment"}} and discard the calls whose arguments are invalid.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. any tells Claude that it must call one of the provided tools on every request, and a forced call leaves no room for a text reply before it. A turn that needs no lookup therefore comes back as a tool call with invented arguments and nothing for the helper to show. Option B returns to the default, auto, which lets Claude decide on each turn whether a tool is needed and answer in text when it is not; its system prompt line on which questions require a lookup covers the incident that led to the forced setting. Option A cannot work, because under any a call is required whatever the descriptions say. Option C changes how text is read, but these responses contain no text part. Option D forces one named tool on every turn, which produces more invented calls and no reply. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say the newest Claude models reject any and named-tool choices with a 400 error, which leaves auto and none. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • Define tools — Forcing tool use • ToolChoice — Converse API reference (AWS docs)

fields.Front: A document-intake eval your team runs has 300 labeled test cases. Each pairs a claim letter with a reference loss_summary that an adjuster wrote: two sentences on what happened, when and where. A model grader reads each generated summary beside its reference and assigns a 1 to 10 score; its whole instruction is "Rate the quality of this summary." Spot checks find it awarding 8 out of 10 to fluent summaries that give the wrong cause of loss, and 5 out of 10 to accurate summaries that are worded unlike the reference. How should grading be changed for this field? A. Grade the field in code by comparing the normalized text of each summary with the reference summary written for that letter. B. Keep the model grader and instruct it to be strict and to reserve its high scores for the summaries it is highly confident in. C.
