Keep the model grader and move it to a larger model that works out for itself what a good loss summary contains. D. Keep the model grader and give it criteria that score agreement with the letter on cause, date and place, not on wording.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Both mis-scores trace to an instruction that never says what "quality" means: the grader rewards fluency and penalises wording because nothing tells it that agreement with the letter on the facts is the point. Explicit criteria fix that, so option D names the facts that have to match and takes wording out of the score. Option A suits a field with one expected value, such as an amount or a date; a free-text summary is right in many wordings, so a text comparison with the reference would fail the accurate summaries. Option B sets a general bar of strictness and confidence without naming what to check, so the grader would go on judging fluency and wording. Option C asks a bigger model to guess requirements that the team is able to state outright. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Tips for LLM-based grading • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Grade your evaluations

fields.Front:
A support team runs an automated QA reviewer built on Claude that reads closed chat transcripts and flags problems for team leads in four categories: skipped identity checks, wrong refund amounts, unapproved exceptions and tone. Leads dismiss 5% to 8% of the flags in the first, second and fourth categories. For unapproved exceptions they dismiss 36%, and nearly all of those dismissed flags are goodwill credits under $25, which written policy lets an agent grant without approval. The prompt's criterion for that category reads "Flag any credit or exception that was granted without a supervisor's approval." Leads act on the rest of that category's flags.

What should the team do first?

A. Switch the unapproved-exceptions category off until its criteria are redesigned, and keep the other three running.
B. Add to that category's criterion that goodwill credits under $25 are allowed without approval and are not flagged.
C. Add an instruction to be conservative and to flag an exception when the reviewer is highly confident of a violation.
D. Have the reviewer attach a confidence score to each flag, and hide the flags that score below a chosen threshold.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The false positives are one known pattern, and the prompt creates them: its criterion says to flag any credit granted without approval, while written policy allows small goodwill credits. A criterion that states what to skip as well as what to report removes them, so option B adds the exception that policy already defines. Option A is the right response when a noisy category cannot be fixed quickly; here the fix is one sentence, and switching the category off would also stop the flags that leads act on. Options C and D both lean on the reviewer's confidence, but a goodwill credit without approval matches the criterion as written, so the reviewer flags it with full confidence and neither a general instruction nor a score threshold would remove it. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Code Review — What you can tune • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

fields.Front: A claims pipeline your team runs on Bedrock extracts fields from intake emails with a dedicated record_intake tool. Its input schema lists adjuster_name under required with the type string, and the prompt says to return null for that field when the email names no adjuster. 18% of emails name none. For those emails the tool input never contains null: it carries an empty string, the text "N/A" or, in 3% of cases, a name taken from the email signature. Downstream code treats any non-empty string as a valid assignment. What is the most effective change? A. Declare adjuster_name with the type ["string", "null"] in the schema, and route null to manual assignment. B. Move the null rule for adjuster_name to the top of the prompt, and route null to manual assignment. C. Add a pattern for personal names to adjuster_name, and reject each tool input whose value does not match it. D. Run the extraction twice for each email, and accept adjuster_name when both calls return the same string.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The prompt already asks for null, yet no tool input contains it, because the schema declares adjuster_name as a required string and leaves no valid way to say that the adjuster is absent. Faced with that contract, Claude fills the field with a placeholder or a plausible name. Option A makes the field nullable in the schema, which gives absence a legitimate value, and its routing of null to manual assignment gives downstream code a clear signal. Option B gives more prominence to an instruction that the schema contradicts, so the conflict remains. Option C checks the shape of the value, which a name from the signature passes, and it offers no value for an email without an adjuster. Option D doubles the cost while both calls face the same required string and are free to agree on the same invented name. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Structured outputs — JSON Schema limitations • Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies • Define tools — Specifying client tools

fields.Front: A document intake system your team runs labels each incoming form through a classify_form tool whose form_type field is an enum of the 14 internal form types, and routing code sends each form to a queue by matching that label exactly. About once a month the business introduces a form type that is not in the enum. Such forms carry a clearly printed title, for example "Salvage Release", yet until the schema is edited Claude assigns them the closest of the 14 listed types. 3% of forms reach the wrong queue, and the team learns of a new type when a queue owner complains. Which change best handles the new form types? A. Replace the enum with a flexible toJSON tool that takes open input, and list the 14 form types in the prompt. B. Add unclear to the enum, and send each form that receives that value to a separate queue for manual review. C. Add other to the enum with a form_type_detail string that holds the printed title, and route other to a review queue. D. Change form_type from an enum to a free-text string, and let Claude write the title that is printed on each form.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The new forms are not ambiguous: each has a clearly printed title that is simply absent from the 14 values, and a closed enum leaves Claude nothing to pick except the nearest wrong type. An other value plus a detail string makes the category list extensible: the known types keep exact labels for routing, and each new type is captured by name and sent to review until the enum is updated. That is option C. Option A gives up the schema's control over the label, so routing by exact match would receive free-form values. Option B describes a different case, a form whose type cannot be determined, and it records nothing about what the new type is. Option D makes every label free text, so the 14 known types would arrive in varying spellings that the routing code does not match. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Define tools — Specifying client tools • Structured outputs — JSON Schema limitations
